summaries.example: Imagine a dog named Clover. In our world she has four legs. We can ask whether there is a possible world—a way things might have been—in which Clover had three legs. One answer says Clover herself exists in both worlds, with different numbers of legs. Another answer says only a similar dog exists in the other world. The puzzle is about which answer best explains what Clover could have been like.
summaries.summary: Transworld identity is the philosophical idea that the same object exists in more than one possible world. A possible world is a way things could have been, and the actual world counts as one of them. This idea helps explain claims such as “Clover could have had three legs.” But philosophers disagree about what it means for a real individual to exist in another possible world. Some think the individual is present there with different properties. David Lewis instead defended counterpart theory: an individual exists in one world, while a similar counterpart in another world makes a claim about what that individual could have been true. Different pictures of possible worlds create different problems. Theories must also explain how an object can change some features without becoming a different object. Puzzles about people, trees, and bicycles show why the issue is difficult, and philosophy has no single accepted solution.
key_ideas: Possible worlds help philosophers talk about what could have happened and what had to happen.
Transworld identity says that the same individual can exist in different possible worlds.
Some philosophers prefer counterpart theory: a thing exists in one world, while similar things in other worlds explain what it could have been like.
The disagreement becomes difficult when an object could have had some different features but not just any features.
There is no agreed final answer about which theory is best.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic asks a basic question about sameness: what makes something the same thing when we imagine it differently? It connects everyday questions about changing objects with bigger questions about possibility, necessity, and identity. Learning the debate also shows how one simple idea can lead to several competing explanations.

important_terms.definition: A possible way the world might have been. Philosophers use possible worlds to discuss what could or could not happen.
The idea that one and the same thing exists in more than one possible world.
A relation of similarity between things in different possible worlds. In this view, a thing exists in only one world but has similar counterparts elsewhere.
A feature that a thing could not lack while still being that very thing.

questions_to_think_about: If a bicycle had different wheels, would it still be the same bicycle?
Can something stay the same while changing some of its features?
Is a very similar object in another world enough to explain what you could have been like?
What features of a person or object, if any, could never change?

summaries.example: Suppose an actual bicycle is built from frame A1 and wheels B1 and C1. It seems possible that the same bicycle began with A1, B1, and a replacement wheel C2. It may also seem possible for that bicycle to have begun with A1, a different wheel B2, and C2. If identity across worlds is transitive, these claims can make the last bicycle identical with the original. Yet we may also want to say that a bicycle could not have begun with almost none of its original parts. The tolerance and restriction principles therefore create a tension that counterpart theory can avoid because similarity need not be transitive.
summaries.summary: Transworld identity is the claim that one and the same individual exists in more than one possible world. Within a possible-worlds framework, it offers a direct interpretation of de re modal claims: saying that a particular person could have had another career becomes saying that the person exists in a world where that career occurs. The view is controversial because the nature of possible worlds matters. On a concrete-world account associated with Lewis, an individual’s presence in more than one world is difficult to understand, so Lewis uses counterpart theory instead. On abstract-world accounts, existence in another world can be understood more deflationarily, as the individual’s having existed had a different complete way the world might have been actual. Further problems remain. Leibniz’s Law must be reconciled with different properties across worlds; arguments about role switching and reduplication raise the possibility of ungrounded or “bare” identities; and transitivity arguments about bicycles place pressure on claims about essential origins. Proposed responses include individual essences, counterpart theory, restrictions on accessibility between worlds, and other revisions. The entry concludes that no consensus has settled the comparative merits of these approaches.
key_ideas: Possible-worlds semantics naturally raises the question of how to interpret modal claims about particular individuals, such as whether a named person could have had a different career.
Transworld identity treats the individual in the other world as numerically the same individual; counterpart theory explains the claim through a similar individual in another world.
Leibniz’s Law does not by itself rule out transworld identity, since identity through time also allows an individual to have different properties at different times.
The debate over criteria of identity distinguishes ways of recognizing an identity from metaphysical conditions that make an identity hold.
Chisholm-style role-switching and Forbes-style reduplication arguments suggest that transworld identity may require individual essences or may involve bare identities.

Bicycle puzzles involving the transitivity of identity create further pressure, and philosophers disagree about whether to revise claims about origins, possible worlds, or the theory of identity itself.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate clarifies what philosophers mean by “could have been otherwise.” It is not enough to list alternative descriptions; we must ask whether an alternative contains the same individual, a similar counterpart, or merely a different arrangement of properties. The issue therefore links modal logic with metaphysics, theories of essence, identity through time, and the status of possible worlds.

important_terms.definition: A statement about what is possible or necessary for a particular object, rather than a claim about what is possible or necessary in general.
The principle that if A and B are identical, they share every property, properly understood with attention to time or world.
A property or group of properties that is necessary and sufficient for being one particular individual in every possible world where that individual exists.
An identity across worlds that is not grounded in other qualitative facts about the individuals involved.
The view that possible worlds differ in ways involving which individuals exist, even when their qualitative features are duplicated.
The view that an individual exists in one possible world but has counterparts in other worlds; the counterpart relation is based on similarity rather than identity.

questions_to_think_about: Does understanding that someone could have had a different career require a full criterion of identity across worlds?
Should an object’s origin be an essential feature, or could it have begun from different materials?
Would a world differing only in which individuals occupy certain roles be genuinely possible?
Is a counterpart relation an adequate replacement for identity, given that similarity may not be transitive?
Which is more costly: accepting bare identities or rejecting some intuitive claims about what objects could have been?

summaries.example: Think about a favorite game character, Mira. In the story we know, Mira becomes a scientist. You might say, “Mira could have become a musician instead.” Does that mean Mira herself appears in another possible world as a musician? A transworld-identity theorist says yes. A counterpart theorist says Mira exists only in our world, but a very similar Mira in another world becomes a musician. The two ideas agree about what could have happened, but they explain it differently.
summaries.summary: Transworld identity means identity across possible worlds: the same object exists in more than one way things could have been. The idea is used to explain statements about particular things, such as “Mira could have become a musician.” If this is translated into possible-world language, it seems to say that Mira exists in a world where she is a musician. But philosophers disagree about whether that is the right interpretation. David Lewis’s counterpart theory says that Mira exists in only one world and has a similar counterpart in another world. The dispute depends partly on what possible worlds are. They might be concrete alternate universes, or they might be abstract descriptions of complete ways the world could have been. The debate also asks whether we need criteria that identify an individual across worlds. Some philosophers say that we can understand and refer to such claims without having a special test. Others worry that, without individual essences, transworld identity allows identities that are not explained by any other facts. Puzzles involving role switching and replacement bicycle parts show the pressure on the theory. Several responses are available, but there is no settled winner.
key_ideas: Philosophers use possible worlds to analyze claims about possibility and necessity.
Transworld identity says an individual can exist in several worlds, while counterpart theory says each individual belongs to one world and has similar counterparts elsewhere.
The question is not only whether we can understand modal claims, but also what makes the same individual present in another world.
Some philosophers argue that we do not need a special test for recognizing or understanding transworld identity claims.
Other arguments suggest that identities across worlds need deeper grounds, such as individual essences, to prevent strange role-switching cases.
Problems about changing bicycle parts show why the debate remains unsettled.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps us separate two questions: what could happen to a particular thing, and what counts as that very thing in an imagined alternative. It also shows why philosophers examine the hidden assumptions behind ordinary sentences. A sentence that sounds simple—“this object could have been different”—can involve theories of worlds, properties, reference, and identity.

important_terms.definition: A complete way things might have been, used to reason about possibilities and necessities.
The claim that one individual can exist in more than one possible world.
A claim about what could or could not be true of one particular thing, such as whether Mira could have chosen another career.
The idea that an individual has similar versions in other possible worlds, rather than literally existing in those worlds.
A feature that belongs to something in every possible world in which it exists.
A special set of essential features that would be enough to identify one individual across possible worlds.

questions_to_think_about: When you imagine a person making a different choice, are you imagining that same person or a similar person?
Why might changing properties across worlds seem to conflict with Leibniz’s Law?
Would a unique origin, such as coming from one particular seed, help identify a tree across worlds?
Can two possible worlds be alike in every noticeable way but differ in which individual is present?
Why might a relation based on similarity avoid a problem that identity creates?
